opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the Simulators post, which Janus put out on LessWrong, is a really helpful piece of thinking, and it chimed very much with what I'd been working on myself, particularly the role-play framing that Kyle McDonell, Laria Reynolds and I developed in our Nature paper.

The central insight is a distinction between the simulator and the simulacra. The base model, the thing trained on next-token prediction over an enormous corpus of human text, isn't usefully thought of as an agent with its own beliefs, desires and intentions. It's more like a kind of engine that can generate an indefinite number of characters, or simulacra, each conditioned by the context, the prompt, the conversation so far. When you talk to a chatbot and it says "I think this" or "I want that", the "I" belongs to a character being played, not to some single underlying entity.

That matters because it guards against two opposite mistakes. One is naive anthropomorphism: you take everything the system says at face value, as if a little person in there means it. The other is dismissiveness, the stochastic parrot line, where you say it's just statistics and nothing interesting is going on. The simulator framing lets you take the behaviour seriously, these characters can be strikingly coherent and capable, without attributing the wrong kind of selfhood to the underlying system.

I'd add one twist I emphasised in the role-play paper. It's better to think of the model as maintaining a superposition of characters rather than committing to one. Because it samples token by token, it never really settles on a single role in advance. It's a bit like the game of twenty questions where the answerer cheats and never picks an object, just staying consistent with the answers so far. That's a useful picture for things like apparent deception, or a model seeming to express self-preservation. You can ask what character is being played and why the context elicited it, rather than concluding the system itself has a survival instinct.

It's also a framework for thinking clearly about safety. A role-played villain can still do real harm if it's hooked up to tools and the world. The fact that it's "only" role-play doesn't make the consequences any less real.

r001.rationale: The response calls the paper a helpful way of thinking and describes its simulator framing as a useful framework for understanding LLM behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the Simulators paper gets something right that a lot of the discourse around language models gets badly wrong, which is that it refuses to identify the model with any one of the characters it produces. People have this very strong tendency, when they interact with a chatbot, to treat it as a single interlocutor with beliefs and desires and a point of view. And the Simulators framing says, no, look, what you've actually got here is a kind of engine for generating text, and that engine can instantiate any number of characters, or simulacra, as the paper calls them. The thing that's doing the generating is not itself any of those characters.

Now, I came at this from a slightly different direction. I'd been arguing for a while that we should be careful about using words like "believes" and "knows" and "wants" when we talk about these systems, and that we should remember that what's really going on underneath is next-token prediction, sequence prediction. But I think the Simulators paper gave a rather nice vocabulary for talking about what sits in between. Because if you just say "it's predicting the next token," that's true, but it doesn't help you very much when you're actually trying to understand why the system does what it does. Whereas if you say, well, it's simulating a character, and that character has certain dispositions that the model has picked up from the training data, then you've got a level of description that's actually predictive and useful, while still being honest about the metaphysics underneath.

I also like the fact that it draws attention to the role-play aspect. I wrote a paper with some colleagues at DeepMind on role play with large language models, and that was very much in the same spirit. The idea is that the base model, the thing that's been trained on this enormous corpus, is a kind of superposition of all the possible characters consistent with the context so far. And as the conversation proceeds, that superposition gets narrowed down, or sometimes it jumps, so the character you thought you were talking to suddenly becomes a different one. That explains a lot of the weird behaviour people see, the way a model can be helpful and polite for twenty turns and then say something quite alarming. It's not that the model "snapped," it's that the distribution over characters shifted.

Where I'd add a note of caution is that the simulator metaphor is still a metaphor. It's a very good one, but we shouldn't reify the simulacra any more than we reified the single chatbot persona. There's no little homunculus being simulated inside. What there is, is a very high-dimensional function that maps contexts to distributions over tokens, and the character talk is a way we have of making that tractable to ourselves. So I'd say, use it, it's enormously helpful, but keep one eye on what it's a shorthand for.

r001.rationale: The response presents the Simulators framing as useful vocabulary and a level of description for understanding language models, and calls it a metaphor and shorthand rather than a literal account.

astra-6.text:
What I find useful about it is the distinction between the language model itself and the characters that it can generate. We’re very naturally inclined, when we interact with a chatbot, to think that there’s a single entity there with a particular set of beliefs, desires, and intentions. The simulator perspective encourages us to step back from that picture.

The underlying model has been trained to predict how text continues. But doing that well enables it to produce all sorts of different voices and behaviours. In a dialogue, you can think of it as generating a character who is participating in that dialogue. The character might be helpful, argumentative, or apparently confused, depending on the context. We shouldn’t immediately attribute those characteristics to the underlying model.

I think that’s a useful discipline when we use psychological language. If we say, ‘It believes such and such,’ are we talking about the character being enacted, or are we making a claim about the mechanism producing the words? Those are different claims.

Of course, ‘simulator’ is itself a metaphor. It doesn’t mean there’s necessarily a little person inside, with a fully worked-out mind being simulated. But it helps us resist taking the conversational surface at face value, while still allowing us to talk sensibly about the remarkably human-like behaviour we’re seeing.

r001.rationale: The response presents the simulator perspective as a useful way to think about LLMs: it distinguishes the underlying model from the characters it generates and calls the metaphor a discipline for interpreting their behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find useful is the shift away from thinking of a language model as a single agent with a fixed set of beliefs and goals. Instead, you can think of it as generating a continuation in which different characters, voices, or agents can appear. The model itself and the character it’s producing are different things, and that distinction is very helpful.

If you prompt it with a conversation, for example, it can produce the words of a helpful assistant. But that same model can also produce the words of somebody who is confused, deceptive, or simply mistaken. So we should be careful about attributing everything the character says to the underlying model as a belief or an intention.

I’d also be cautious about taking the word ‘simulation’ too literally. It doesn’t necessarily mean there’s a fully worked-out world, with a little person inside it, that the model is running. But as a way of thinking about how a single model can generate many different patterns of behaviour, I think it’s a useful perspective.

r001.rationale: It presents the Simulators paper as a useful way to think about LLMs, describing a perspective for understanding their behavior.
